entry.title: CockroachDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine Built to Survive Anything

link.title: CockroachDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine Built to Survive Anything

entry.content:
If you are serving AI features to users in several regions at once, you eventually hit the same wall: a single-node Postgres works beautifully until you need writes to survive a datacenter failure, or until feature data, embeddings metadata, and audit trails have to stay transactionally consistent across continents. CockroachDB is the open-source answer that industry keeps reaching for — a distributed SQL database written in Go that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, scales horizontally by splitting data into replicated ranges, and refuses to lose an acknowledged write even when machines are failing underneath it. For ML platforms specifically, it is a natural backing store for regional feature stores, vector-metadata joins, and anything where a stale or lost row quietly corrupts a model’s inputs.

What makes it fascinating to read at the source level is how little magic there is. Everything reduces to one repeated loop: a SQL statement becomes a transactional batch of key-value requests, that batch is routed to a leaseholder replica, the replica evaluates it against multi-version MVCC state, the result is replicated through Raft, and the whole thing rests on an LSM-tree engine called Pebble. If you have followed our earlier storage-engine tours of RocksDB and LevelDB, you will feel at home immediately — Pebble is the direct Go descendant of that same LSM lineage, purpose-built by Cockroach Labs when they outgrew embedding RocksDB as a C++ library inside their Go process.

In this tour we read the actual code in the cockroachdb/cockroach monorepo and draw two architecture diagrams from it: an overview of the full query path, and a detailed map of the functions that make it work. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the current master branch, so the links drop you straight into the source.

Overview: one query's journey from a Postgres-compatible socket to replicated LSM storage. Every edge is a real call path in the Go source.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A session is just a wire protocol. The pgwire conn struct (conn, L59) accepts the same PostgreSQL frontend/backend protocol that Postgres speaks, so existing drivers connect with zero code changes. Server.ServeConn (ServeConn, L991) upgrades each connection into a SQL session.
  • Sessions run a state machine. connExecutor (connExecutor, L1609) owns transaction state, and execStmt (execStmt, L123) with execStmtInOpenState (execStmtInOpenState, L417) drive every statement through it.
  • Every query is optimized, not interpreted. planner.makeOptimizerPlan (makeOptimizerPlan, L298) builds a memo of alternative plans and prices them; coster.ComputeCost (coster.ComputeCost, L526) is where join orders and index choices actually get decided.
  • Plans become physical flows. The PhysicalPlan (PhysicalPlan, L125) assigns operators to nodes, and flows of ProcessorBase instances (ProcessorBase, L345) execute them locally or distributed.
  • SQL touches data only through KV. Row sources end up in Txn.Send (Txn.Send, L1386), which funnels batches into the TxnCoordSender (TxnCoordSender, L510) for intent tracking and retries.
  • Batches are routed, not broadcast. DistSender.Send (DistSender.Send, L1310) splits a BatchRequest by key range and sendToReplicas (sendToReplicas, L2669) targets each range’s leaseholder replica over gRPC.
  • One Node fronts one process. Inbound RPCs land in Node.batchInternal (batchInternal, L1648), which hands work to the Store (Store, L909) that owns replicas on local disks.
  • Replicas evaluate, then replicate. The Replica (Replica, L365) evaluates the batch under its lease, and evalAndPropose (evalAndPropose, L116) proposes the result to Raft so a majority durably agrees.
  • Everything ends in Pebble. The Pebble engine (Pebble, L884) implements the Engine interface (Engine, L932) and persists both the Raft log and the MVCC keyspace.

The detailed map: 34 components from wire protocol to LSM compactions, with the exact functions that glue each layer to the next.

SQL: From Wire Protocol to Costed Memo

The SQL layer’s discipline is striking: there is exactly one optimizer, and nothing bypasses it. optbuilder.Builder.Build (Builder.Build, L263) converts the parsed AST into a memo — a DAG of relational expressions where equivalent alternatives share groups. The xform explorer then applies transformation rules via exploreGroup (exploreGroup, L155) until the Coster (coster.ComputeCost, L526) can no longer find a cheaper expression. Cost here is not an abstract score: it is calibrated in units of IO, CPU, and memory (the Cost type lives in Cost, L17), which is why the optimizer can reason sensibly about wide scans of embedding tables versus narrow index lookups on feature keys.

Execution follows the same decomposition. dispatchToExecutionEngine (dispatchToExecutionEngine, L2887) picks between local and distributed plans, execWithDistSQLEngine (execWithDistSQLEngine, L3664) sets up flows, and each node runs its fragment through the Flow interface (Flow, L72). Processors stream rows to each other rather than materializing whole tables — the same pull-based style that makes DuckDB-class engines cache-friendly.

KV: TxnCoordSender and the DistSender

Beneath SQL, CockroachDB is a transactional key-value store, and the client side of that store is small enough to hold in your head. kv.DB (DB, L272) hands out Txn handles; batches stage operations like Batch.Put (Batch.Put, L460) as kvpb requests. The TxnCoordSender (TxnCoordSender, L510) is the transaction’s brain: it records which ranges hold intents, heartbeats the transaction record so other nodes can tell a live writer from a crashed one, and orchestrates retries.

The DistSender (DistSender, L726) then does geography: it consults the range metadata to find which leaseholder serves each key span, splits the batch accordingly, and re-runs pieces when ranges split or leaders move mid-flight. By default every transaction runs at SERIALIZABLE isolation — the strongest level Postgres only offers opt-in — implemented through MVCC timestamps and read refreshes rather than lock tables.

Replication: Ranges, Leases, and Raft

Each range (a contiguous key span, default 512 MiB) is owned by a Replica on each of its three or more voting stores. Exactly one replica holds the lease at a time; pendingLeaseRequest.requestLease (requestLease, L552) and its async variant (requestLeaseAsync, L474) make acquisition cooperative and liveness-aware. Only the leaseholder may serve consistent reads, which is why the diagram routes every batch through it.

Writes then follow classic Raft. evaluateBatch (evaluateBatch, L198) runs the batch against current state to produce a result; evalAndPropose (evalAndPropose, L116) turns that into a proposed command with a MaxLeaseIndex for replay protection; propose (propose, L411) enqueues it; and handleRaftReady (handleRaftReady, L867) drains the ready data into the log and transport. The consensus algorithm itself lives in the vendored pkg/raft library (raft, L305), a heavily-evolved descendant of etcd’s raft. Acknowledgment waits for a majority, so a range survives losing a minority of its replicas with no human intervention.

Storage: MVCC over a Pebble LSM

The storage engine contract is the Engine interface (Engine, L932) — a versioned reader/writer — and Pebble is its production implementation (Pebble, L884). MVCC keys are literally user keys suffixed with wall-clock timestamps, so MVCCGet (MVCCGet, L1401) and MVCCPut (MVCCPut, L1923) are LSM operations over that encoding, with mvccPutInternal (mvccPutInternal, L2251) deciding between values and tombstoned intents. Scans merge intents and versions through pebbleMVCCScanner (pebbleMVCCScanner, L381).

This is the part of the codebase our series has been circling for months: Pebble takes the LSM ideas RocksDB refined from LevelDB — memtables, tiered SSTables, bloom filters, compactions — and re-implements them in pure Go, adding level-aware write amplification control that suits CockroachDB’s raft-append-heavy workload. Reading pkg/storage right after those two codebases is a genuinely satisfying experience.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything below comes straight from the repository’s own README. The quickest route is a pre-built binary: the README’s “Starting with CockroachDB” list points at the documented installer page for your platform. If you would rather build from source, the README’s “Building from source” section defers to the project wiki; expect a Bazel-driven build — the repo’s GNUmakefile is a thin wrapper whose build target just runs ./dev build, and ./dev in turn drives Bazel. Budget real time and disk for the first compile; this is a large monorepo with C dependencies.

Once you have a cockroach binary: start a local demo cluster with three nodes as the README suggests, open the built-in SQL client, create a database and table, and then connect your application with any PostgreSQL driver or ORM — the README explicitly notes that the PostgreSQL wire protocol is supported, so psycopg2, asyncpg, or SQLAlchemy all work unchanged. For an ML service, your first schema might be a features table keyed by entity ID with an _updated_at column, giving you transactional feature reads alongside the labels you train on.

Honest Limits

Read the license before you plan around it. Since the v24.3 series (releases after November 18, 2024, per the README’s licensing section), the code ships under the CockroachDB Software License rather than an OSI-approved open-source license: the LICENSE file grants use and modification for operating, testing, and improving CockroachDB, but prohibits offering it as a commercial DBaaS without a license key. Source-available, yes; fully open-source, no. For an internal AI platform this is usually irrelevant, but check it before embedding.

Engineering costs are real, too. The monorepo is enormous (over 20,000 tracked files), builds run through Bazel with a custom ./dev tool, and running a production cluster means operating at least three nodes, monitoring Raft health, and accepting that every write pays a consensus round-trip. It is a server, not an embeddable library — there is no “just link it into your app” mode like SQLite’s. For single-region workloads that fit in one machine, plain Postgres remains simpler; for battery-backup-grade regional consistency, that trade is exactly what you are buying.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of CockroachDB's Go monorepo, tracing a query from the PostgreSQL wire protocol through the cost-based optimizer, the DistSender, Raft replication, and down into the Pebble LSM storage engine.

entry.title: LevelDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Engine That Started It All

link.title: LevelDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Engine That Started It All

entry.content:
Yesterday we walked the RocksDB source tree — the heavily forked engine that powers Flink state stores, Kafka Streams, TiKV, and the local segments of countless vector databases. But RocksDB did not appear out of nothing. It is a fork of LevelDB, the compact key-value library written at Google by Sanjay Ghemawat and Jeff Dean. The README describes it modestly: “a fast key-value storage library written at Google that provides an ordered mapping from string keys to string values.” Behind that one line sits the first widely read implementation of the log-structured merge (LSM) architecture — append-only writes, sorted in-memory tables, immutable disk files, and background compaction. Every storage engine that calls itself LSM today is quoting this codebase, usually without attribution.

Why should an ML or data-infrastructure engineer care about a ~20k-line C++ library? Because embedded KV stores are the substrate under a surprising amount of AI plumbing. Feature stores and data-preparation jobs use them as durable, ordered dictionaries for raw events and materialized features. On-device inference stacks use them as local caches and model registries, and the browser world famously runs on this lineage too — Chrome’s IndexedDB is backed by LevelDB, which means every offline-first ML web app ultimately reads and writes one of these files. Stream-processing frameworks checkpoint operator state into RocksDB descendants of this exact design. Once you understand how LevelDB turns a Put into a log record, a skiplist insert, and eventually a sorted string table, half the storage engines you will ever debug become familiar.

This post tours google/leveldb at its main branch, verified line by line in the actual source. Two diagrams anchor the tour: an overview of the full write-and-read cycle, and a detail view that expands into the individual functions. All paths below are repo-relative, so you can open any link and land on the exact function we discuss.

The complete LevelDB cycle: every write is logged, absorbed by a skiplist memtable, spilled into an immutable Level-0 SSTable, merged across levels by background compaction, and coordinated through the version set and MANIFEST file. Reads probe the newest structures first.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • DBImpl::Write, L1206 is the only write entry point. It queues the writer, merges concurrent small batches via DBImpl::BuildBatchGroup, L1281, and performs the canonical LSM handshake: log first, memory second.
  • log::Writer::AddRecord, L34 appends the batch to the write-ahead log, fragmenting records across 32KB physical blocks with per-fragment CRC checksums.
  • WriteBatchInternal::InsertInto, L132 replays the batch through a handler that lands each operation in the memtable via MemTable::Add, L76 — keys stamped with a sequence number and a value-or-deletion type tag.
  • DBImpl::MakeRoomForWrite, L1331 enforces the 4MB memtable budget (write_buffer_size, options.h, L83) and switches the active memtable to immutable before handing writes to a fresh one.
  • DBImpl::WriteLevel0Table, L505 and BuildTable, L17 flush the immutable memtable into a brand-new SSTable using TableBuilder::Add, L94, which emits restart-point compressed data blocks.
  • DBImpl::BackgroundCompaction, L708 runs on a single background thread, consuming the compaction score computed by VersionSet::PickCompaction, L1252.
  • VersionSet::LogAndApply, L777 publishes every file-level change — flushes and compactions alike — as a VersionEdit appended to the MANIFEST.
  • DBImpl::Get, L1121 probes memtable, immutable memtable, then the live file set through Version::Get, L324, newest structure first, stopping at the first match.

The detail view expands each stage into its constituent functions: batch grouping and replay, the skiplist-plus-arena memory stack, 32KB log blocks and recovery, the SSTable format from TableBuilder to BlockIter, the level-by-level read probe, score-driven compaction, and the bloom-filter and LRU-cache shields that keep reads off disk.

The Write Path: Log First, Skiplist Second

The elegance of DBImpl::Write is its group-commit queue. Each calling thread registers a Writer on a deque and sleeps until it reaches the front. The leader then calls BuildBatchGroup to absorb pending writers into one merged batch (capped at 1MB, plus 128KB when the first batch is small), stamps it with the next sequence numbers, and — with the lock released — appends it via log_->AddRecord and applies it through WriteBatchInternal::InsertInto. This is why a single-item write and a thousand-item batch cost roughly the same number of fsyncs: batching is the engine’s answer to write amplification at the front door.

The memtable itself is a skiplist, not a balanced tree. SkipList::Insert, L55 relies on the arena allocator (Arena::AllocateAligned, L38) so that nodes are only reclaimed wholesale when the entire memtable dies. MemTable::Add encodes each entry as key length | sequence<<8 | type | key | value length | value, which makes iteration order deterministic even for duplicate user keys. Readers traverse the same structure with MemTable::Get, L102, and the exported MemTableIterator, L46 doubles as a compaction input.

Recovery is the mirror image: at open time, DBImpl::RecoverLogFile, L385 replays the last WAL into a fresh memtable, which is why every committed Put survives a crash even though the memtable was pure memory.

Reading: One Probe, Three Frontiers, Then Levels

DBImpl::Get assembles a LookupKey with the current sequence number and hands it to Version::Get, L324. Level 0 is special: its files can overlap each other, so all of them are searched newest-first. From level 1 upward, files are key-disjoint, and the version binary-searches for the single file whose range brackets the key — typically one file touched per level. Before any data block is read, the bloom filter answers cheaply: FilterBlockReader::KeyMayMatch, L90 consults a per-block filter built from BloomFilterPolicy, L17 at roughly ten bits per key, so absent keys skip both the file read and the block decode.

When a block is actually needed, TableCache::Get, L100 opens the file through Table::Open, L38, and Table::InternalGet, L214 seeks the index block, loads the data block, and scans it with the iterator from Block::NewIterator, L280. Two caches amortize this work: the table cache holds open file handles, and ShardedLRUCache, L353 — sixteen independent LRU lists with LRUCache::Insert, L268 as the hot path — keeps decompressed blocks in memory. The README’s own db_bench numbers make the effect concrete: readrandom improves from about 60,000 to about 190,000 reads per second once compaction and block caching warm up.

Iteration composes the same pieces: NewMergingIterator, L179 unions the memtable iterator with one iterator per file level, and DBIter, L39 filters internal keys and tombstones so the user sees a clean ordered view. Telemetry hooks like DBImpl::GetApproximateSizes, L1469 round out the API by summing file sizes overlapping a key range — the same primitive monitoring tools use to chart database growth.

Compaction and the Version Set

Compaction is where LSM engines earn their name. VersionSet::PickCompaction, L1252 scores every level and picks the worst offender; Level 0 compacts when it accumulates four files, while deeper levels compact on a size ratio. DBImpl::DoCompactionWork, L898 then merges the inputs with a MergingIterator, dropping entries shadowed by newer versions or tombstones (it consults Compaction::IsBaseLevelForKey to know whether a tombstone can finally be discarded) and writing outputs sized to the level’s file budget — 2MB default files per max_file_size in options.h, L116.

Every mutation of the file universe flows through VersionSet::LogAndApply, L777. The new file lists are assembled by VersionSet::Builder::SaveTo, L672 into a successor Version, the edit is appended to the MANIFEST, and the immutable old version stays alive for any reader still holding a snapshot. This copy-on-write versioning is what makes lock-free reads and consistent snapshots coexist with a mutating database — a design RocksDB inherited wholesale.

From Install to Your First Model

LevelDB builds with CMake out of the box. The README’s POSIX quick start is two commands:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/google/leveldb.git
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release .. && cmake --build .

On Windows, generate a Visual Studio solution with cmake -G "Visual Studio 15 Win64" .. and build it with devenv /build Debug leveldb.sln. Link against the resulting library (and Snappy for compression) and you have your first feature store in a few lines — the same API surface verified in db.h, L53 and options.h, L50:

leveldb::DB* db;
leveldb::Options options;
options.create_if_missing = true;
leveldb::Status s = leveldb::DB::Open(options, "features.db", &db);
db->Put(leveldb::WriteOptions(), "feature:user:42", payload);
std::string value;
db->Get(leveldb::ReadOptions(), "feature:user:42", &value);

Wrap this in Python via one of the mature bindings and you can log training features, deduplicate corpus shards by content hash, or persist inference results with byte-range ordering for free.

Honest Limits

The README is refreshingly blunt about scope, and these limits are exactly why forks exist. LevelDB is not a SQL database — no relational model, no query language, no secondary indexes; you bring the schema logic. Only a single process (possibly multi-threaded) may open a database at a time, and there is no client-server support: networked deployments must wrap their own server. The maintenance posture is worth respecting too — the repository now accepts only critical-bug fixes, so it is a design reference more than a moving product. Operationally, the cost model is asymmetric: the README’s benchmark shows fillsync at 0.4 MB/s versus 62.7 MB/s without per-write syncs, and background compaction trades write latency spikes for read speed — the very tradeoff that RocksDB later tuned with threads and rate limiting, and that LSM-descended time-series engines like the one behind InfluxDB’s storage redesign reshaped for their own workloads.

If you want to go deeper, compare this tour with our RocksDB source walkthrough to see what the fork changed — column families, pluggable memtables, compaction strategies — and with SQLite, the other single-process embedded classic, which chose a B-tree instead of an LSM. Vector-database readers will recognize the pattern too: projects like Milvus build their local mutable-state persistence on RocksDB’s LSM files, the direct descendants of everything diagrammed above.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of google/leveldb tracing the write path, skiplist memtable, WAL, SSTable format, compaction scoring and version sets of the original LSM storage engine.

entry.title: Inside MySQL: A Source-Level Tour of InnoDB, the Optimizer, and Replication

link.title: Inside MySQL: A Source-Level Tour of InnoDB, the Optimizer, and Replication

entry.content:
MySQL is the quiet backbone of the internet. Written in C and C++, maintained by Oracle in the open on GitHub, it has spent three decades being the default transactional database behind forums, e-commerce carts, payment ledgers, and SaaS dashboards. Its storage engine, InnoDB, delivers full ACID transactions, crash recovery through a write-ahead log, and row-level locking — all in a codebase you can clone, grep, and read end to end. For this tour I rendered two architecture diagrams of mysql/mysql-server directly from the source tree, and every claim below links to a real file and line in the repository.

Why should AI engineers care about a 1990s-era SQL server? Because almost every serious LLM application needs one. When your chatbot writes conversation history, your recommendation service logs features, or your billing layer records inference credits, you want a store that is consistent under concurrent writes and survivable across restarts — that is MySQL’s home turf. Feature stores, annotation queues, agent memory, and evaluation harnesses all start as rows in an OLTP table long before anything reaches a vector index. Teams often pair MySQL with Redis as a cache and key-value layer in front of it, or replicate change events into Kafka to feed downstream model training and streaming feature computation. And if you come from the PostgreSQL world, reading MySQL’s source is the fastest way to understand why the two ecosystem cultures differ so much.

The version I read is the development branch: git ls-remote shows the default branch is trunk, and the MYSQL_VERSION file reports 26.10.0-INNOVATION with previous LTS 9.7.0 — so this is moving, forward-looking code, not a packaged release. The full tree lists roughly 61,000 files; I checked out only sql (the server core), storage/innobase (InnoDB), mysys, and libbinlogevents for the diagrams. Here is the big picture, from the network socket down to disk.

MySQL request flow: from mysqld's connection loop through the SQL layer and InnoDB to the binary log and replica threads. Rendered from the trunk tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot and accept. mysqld_main, L9206 initializes engines and enters the connection event loop; each accepted socket goes through Connection_handler_manager::process_new_connection, L262, which hands it to a per-connection handler.
  • Speak the wire protocol. Protocol_classic::get_command, L2890 reads one packet and decodes the COM_* command byte that drives everything else.
  • Parse the query. dispatch_command, L1748 switches on that byte; for COM_QUERY it tokenizes via lex_one_token, L1490 and feeds the bison grammar.
  • Plan it. JOIN::optimize, L344 picks join order, access methods, and temp-table strategies per query block.
  • Compile to iterators. CreateIteratorFromAccessPath, L696 turns the declarative plan into a tree of RowIterator objects, executed by Query_expression::ExecuteIteratorQuery, L1068.
  • Cross the engine boundary. The executor pulls rows through handler::ha_index_read_map, L3390 — the portable storage-engine interface — and writes rows through ha_write_row.
  • Inside InnoDB. Reads funnel into row_search_mvcc, L4437, pages are fetched by buf_page_get_gen, L4473 in the buffer pool, and durability comes from the redo log writer thread.
  • Replicate it. Commit goes through MYSQL_BIN_LOG::ordered_commit, L7530 for binlog group commit, and a dump thread streams events to replica I/O threads.

The detail diagram zooms into the parts that make MySQL genuinely interesting under load: the iterator executor, the InnoDB B-tree and buffer pool machinery, mini-transactions, MVCC, and the three-stage commit.

Internal detail: how a query becomes iterators, how InnoDB pages and redo interact, and how group commit coordinates binlog and engine commits.

From Install to Your First Model

Suppose you want this stack running so an AI service can start writing rows to it. The README in the repo is famously minimal — thirteen lines that state this is a release of MySQL, an SQL database server, and point you at the canonical places: downloads at dev.mysql.com/downloads and documentation at dev.mysql.com/doc. Binary packages from that page are the realistic path for production. If you want to read along with source instead, clone the GitHub repo and build with CMake — the root CMakeLists.txt is the entry point, and the Docs directory in the tree carries the generated documentation sources. Building the whole server is a heavyweight compile, so most readers should install a packaged server and keep the clone open next to the debugger.

Once a server is up, the “first model” of an AI product is usually a feature or metadata table: one row per user interaction, columns for the prompt, the model version, latency, and the outcome label. Standard SQL does the rest — inserts from your service, indexes for the access patterns, and transactions to keep counters and audit rows consistent. The value of the diagrams above is knowing what happens between that INSERT statement and the disk: a protocol packet becomes a parse tree, the optimizer compiles it into iterators, InnoDB inserts into a B-tree under a mini-transaction, and the redo log makes it durable before the client gets its OK.

The InnoDB Write Path: Mini-Transactions and the Redo Log

InnoDB’s unit of crash-safety is the mini-transaction. Every page modification — a row insert, a B-tree split, an undo record — is bracketed by an mtr that accumulates physical log records. When the mtr ends, mtr_t::commit, L577 publishes those records into the log buffer in one atomic step. From there a dedicated writer thread, log_writer_write_buffer, L2123, copies contiguous LSN ranges to the redo files. This is classic write-ahead logging: nothing dirty leaves the buffer pool before the redo that describes it is on disk.

The interplay shows up cleanly in the code. A full leaf page during insert triggers btr_page_split_and_insert, L2315, and the split’s structural changes ride the same mtr discipline as the row data. Meanwhile the page cleaner batches dirty pages with buf_flush_page_and_try_neighbors, L1394, which tries to flush adjacent pages in the same extent so one disk seek amortizes several writes. When memory pressure builds, eviction goes through buf_LRU_free_page, L956, which only frees a page whose redo is already durable. And a checkpointing thread — Log_checkpointing::log_checkpointer, L851 — advances the point from which crash recovery must replay, keeping restart time bounded no matter how far the write volume grows.

MVCC and Locking: Reading Without Blocking

The reason MySQL can serve dashboards and heavy writers from the same tables is multi-version concurrency. Every row carries hidden transaction columns, and a reader opens a snapshot: MVCC::view_open, L489 registers which transactions were active at snapshot time. As row_search_mvcc, L4437 walks an index, it consults that read view and reconstructs older row versions from undo records when a row has been modified after the snapshot began. A long-running analytical query therefore does not stall an insert-hungry ingestion service — the reader just sees the older, consistent world.

Writers, by contrast, use locks. lock_rec_lock, L1849 acquires record-level locks and queues waiters behind conflicting holders; if wait-for edges form a cycle, Deadlock_notifier::notify, L6054 walks the cycle, picks a victim, and rolls it back so the other transaction can proceed. Commit itself ends in trx_commit, L2293, which writes the commit record to redo and releases the locks. Understanding the split — MVCC for readers, locks for writers — explains most MySQL tuning advice you will ever read about isolation levels and gap locking.

The Optimizer and the Iterator Executor

Modern MySQL no longer interprets a parse tree directly. The optimizer’s plan — access paths — is compiled into a composition of row iterators. Leaf iterators such as TableScanIterator::DoRead, L276 wrap the handler calls, while composite iterators like AggregateIterator::DoRead, L290 implement grouping, joins, and materialization by pulling from children. This pull-based design is why EXPLAIN output maps so cleanly onto runtime behavior, and it is the piece to study if you are porting a query layer or benchmarking access patterns for an AI feature store.

Binlog Group Commit and Replication

Durability of a transaction has two halves: the engine’s redo log and the server’s binary log. The two-phase commit coordinator ha_commit_trans, L1686 hands the transaction to the binlog as a TC log via MYSQL_BIN_LOG::commit, L6807. The heart of throughput is MYSQL_BIN_LOG::ordered_commit, L7530: transactions are queued into flush, sync, and commit stages, with change_stage, L7278 serializing each stage so many concurrent writers amortize one fsync. That group commit behavior is why write-heavy AI event logging survives on commodity disks.

Replication is the natural extension: a dump thread running Binlog_sender::run, L386 streams events to each replica, where handle_slave_io, L5439 lands them in a relay log and handle_slave_sql, L7123 applies them. For read-heavy AI dashboards, replicas give you a scale-out read tier; for change-data-capture, the binlog is the feed you tap into with connectors that forward mutations to Kafka or a warehouse.

Honest Limits

  • The README is a pointer, not a manual. It contains no quick-start commands, no build recipes, and no performance claims — just downloads and docs links plus a license note. Everything operational lives at dev.mysql.com, not in the repo.
  • You are reading a moving target. The tree’s MYSQL_VERSION says 26.10.0-INNOVATION after LTS 9.7.0. Innovation releases move fast and carry newer, less battle-tested features; pin a packaged LTS for anything production-facing.
  • Source builds are heavy. The tracked tree is on the order of 61,000 files, and a from-scratch server build is a long CMake compile with sizeable dependencies — fine for study, not a quick afternoon.
  • No vector search out of the box. Unlike some Postgres extensions, MySQL has no native similarity-search index for embeddings; you pair it with a dedicated vector store or use application-level matching, which changes the architecture of embedding-driven features.
  • Replication lag is real. The async dump-and-apply design shown above means replicas trail the source; reading your own writes from a replica after an insert needs application care or semi-sync configurations.

MySQL rewards the time you spend in its source. The next time a feature store query or a replication hiccup puzzles you, the diagrams above give you a map, and the line-anchored links drop you straight into the exact function where the behavior lives.
