entry.title: PostgreSQL Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Engine Powering Your AI Data Layer

link.title: PostgreSQL Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Engine Powering Your AI Data Layer

entry.content:
Ask around any serious ML team and you will hear the same answer to the question “where does your data actually live?”: PostgreSQL. The vector search boom did not replace it — it extended it, with pgvector and friends turning a battle-tested relational engine into the metadata store, embedding index, and retrieval backend for retrieval-augmented generation systems. Search layers such as ParadeDB are built directly on top of Postgres, feature stores use it as their source of truth, and experiment-tracking servers default to it as their persistence layer. The default is not nostalgia: it is the consequence of thirty years of correctness work on transactions, concurrency, and recovery.

What makes that trust interesting is that PostgreSQL is written in C, in the open, in a codebase that has been continuously developed since the 1980s. Nothing in it is hidden behind a vendor wall. When you call SELECT from a client, a forked operating-system process walks your SQL through a real compiler front end, a cost-based optimizer, a tuple-at-a-time executor, a shared buffer pool, and a write-ahead log before anything touches disk. Understanding that path changes how you tune it — why a naive UPDATE-heavy feature table bloats, why connections are expensive, why a checkpoint can cause a latency spike.

This post is a source tour of the postgres/postgres mirror on the master branch. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual tree, and the two diagrams were generated from the same checkout. We follow one query from the wire to the WAL, then step inside the planner, MVCC visibility, recovery, and the maintenance machinery that keeps it all honest. The goal is not to make you a PostgreSQL hacker in one sitting — it is to give you a map accurate enough that when something misbehaves in production, you know which corner of the source to open first.

The life of a query: one client connection, one forked backend, one pass through the SQL compilers, executor, buffer manager, and write-ahead log.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The client never talks to storage. Applications link against libpq, and the connection is established by PQconnectdb, L825, which resolves the conninfo string and runs the startup handshake.
  • One process per connection. The postmaster binds the listen sockets in PostmasterMain, L496 and forks a dedicated backend per client via BackendStartup, L3599 — isolation by process boundary, not threads.
  • The session loop. Each backend lives in exec_simple_query, L1030, the per-statement cycle that parses, plans, executes, and formats results for every string the client sends.
  • Parsing is two stages. raw_parser, L42 turns SQL text into raw parse trees, and transformTopLevelStmt, L265 resolves names and types into a semantically checked Query.
  • Views and policies happen here. The rewriter’s QueryRewrite, L4649 expands views, applies rules, and enforces row security before any cost model sees the query.
  • The optimizer is a search. standard_planner, L357 drives it: make_one_rel, L183 builds access paths per relation, and make_join_rel, L746 enumerates join orders and methods.
  • Execution is a pull chain. ExecutorRun, L308 starts the plan, and nodes like ExecHashJoin, L818 pull tuples upward one at a time.
  • Every change is logged first. Writes go through the heap in heap_insert, L2007 and become durable via XLogInsert, L486 — the record reaches the WAL before the page itself is dirty.

Inside the machine: the optimizer's join search, the executor's node zoo, the buffer pool internals, MVCC visibility, and the background processes for checkpoints and vacuum.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps it deliberately short: get the software from postgresql.org/download, and read the installation documentation for the build from source. Building from the tree confirms why. The Makefile refuses to do anything until you have configured the tree — run ./configure, and only then do the GNU make targets make, make check, and make install become meaningful (the top-level Makefile even prints “You need to run the ‘configure’ program first” if you skip it, and it insists on GNU make specifically). make check runs the regression suite that has guarded executor and planner behavior for decades.

Once installed, the tree’s own tools bootstrap a cluster: initdb (its source lives at src/bin/initdb/initdb.c) creates the data directory, createdb (src/bin/scripts/createdb.c) makes your database, and the interactive terminal psql (src/bin/psql/) connects you. Your first query — a CREATE TABLE for model metadata, a few INSERTs of experiment runs, a SELECT with a join — exercises exactly the path in the overview diagram. For ML use, that first table is often the seed of a feature store: an immutable-events table plus a materialized current-state table, both served by the same engine your notebook already connects to through libpq.

Inside the Planner

PostgreSQL’s optimizer is not a rule engine; it is an explicit search over paths. make_one_rel walks every base relation and produces the candidate access paths — sequential scans, index scans, and their parameterized variants — each annotated with estimated startup and total costs. When a join is possible, make_join_rel considers each join order and method, prunes by cost, and keeps only the cheapest path per relation set. Only after the search converges does create_plan translate the winning Path tree into the Plan nodes the executor actually runs.

The practical consequence for analytics-adjacent ML work is that plan quality is an estimation problem. The planner trusts its statistics; stale statistics after a bulk load of training data can flip a hash join into a nested loop. The standard defense is operational, not architectural: analyze after large loads, and read EXPLAIN before complaining about speed.

MVCC and the Real Cost of an UPDATE

PostgreSQL never overwrites a row in place. An update inserts a new tuple version and marks the old one dead-for-everyone-eventually. Visibility is decided by HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC in src/backend/access/heap/heapam_visibility.c (L939), which inspects the inserting and deleting transaction IDs of each candidate tuple against the reader’s snapshot. Commit status comes from the CLOG, where TransactionIdSetStatusBit (L131) packs four states per transaction into shared bitmaps that every backend consults.

This design is why readers never block writers and writers never block readers — a large property for serving features while backfills run. The price is paid in dead tuples. A feature table updated on every training run accumulates versions that only VACUUM can reclaim; heap_vacuum_rel in src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c (L624) does that scavenging, and the autovacuum launcher (AutoVacWorkerMain, L1413) triggers it by thresholds you can tune per table. Append-only event tables and periodically rebuilt aggregates are the idiomatic way to keep that machinery bored.

WAL: How a Commit Survives a Crash

Durability in PostgreSQL has a strict order: log first, page later. Before a backend modifies any shared page, it assembles a record via XLogInsert and writes it to the WAL buffers; the commit record’s flush is what a returning COMMIT actually waits for. Checkpoints, run by the dedicated checkpointer process (CheckpointerMain, L206) and implemented around CreateCheckPoint in src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c (L7692), force all dirty buffers to disk and write a marker so that recovery never has to replay from the beginning of time.

At startup after a crash, StartupXLOG (L6083, same file) locates the last valid checkpoint and the recovery machinery replays forward, with ApplyWalRecord in src/backend/access/transam/xlogrecovery.c (L1906) re-applying each record’s changes to the pages. The whole scheme means a lost machine loses nothing acknowledged, and it is also the foundation of physical replication — which is how most teams give their metadata store a hot standby.

Where PostgreSQL Fits in an AI Stack

The engine’s role in ML infrastructure is usually “system of record plus retrieval.” With pgvector, embeddings live beside the features they describe, and the planner’s index choices matter as much for ORDER BY embedding <-> $1 LIMIT 10 as for any join. For hybrid lexical-plus-semantic search, ParadeDB adds BM25 scoring and analytics inside Postgres itself rather than exporting data to a separate cluster. For heavy feature computations, a common shape pairs Postgres with DuckDB: transactional truth in Postgres, columnar scanning and vectorized aggregation outside it. A Redis tier in front absorbs hot-path lookups, and if your events are really time-series, QuestDB-style stores can own the high-ingest tail while Postgres keeps the relational core. The point of the diagrams above is that whichever extension you bolt on, it enters through the same parser, planner, and executor everyone else uses — and that is also why extension quality varies so widely. An extension that mishandles the buffer pinning or snapshot rules the core enforces can corrupt state in ways the core cannot see. Prefer extensions that ship in reputable distributions, pin their versions in your infrastructure code, and test them against your real query mix, because the C ABI they ride on is stable but not forgiving.

Honest Limits

Read the source and the trade-offs are visible rather than hidden. First, the process-per-connection model that BackendStartup implements is robust but heavy: thousands of client connections mean thousands of processes, which is why external poolers are near-mandatory at scale. Second, MVCC’s copy-on-write means unvacuumed bloat is a real failure mode, and autovacuum defaults are tuned conservatively — write-heavy tables need attention. Third, the executor pulls tuples one at a time through virtual function calls; this is superb for transactional access and merely adequate for scanning billions of rows, which is why columnar systems and analytical engines exist alongside rather than instead of Postgres. Fourth, planning is only as good as its statistics — the optimizer will confidently misestimate on skewed data. None of these are bugs; they are the design’s edges, and knowing where they are is what separates operating Postgres from merely installing it.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the PostgreSQL C source — from libpq and the postmaster to the planner, the MVCC heap, and the write-ahead log — with architecture diagrams that show how the world's most trusted open-source database really runs.

entry.title: RocksDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Storage Engine Behind Modern Infrastructure

link.title: RocksDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Storage Engine Behind Modern Infrastructure

entry.content:
RocksDB is the storage engine you have probably used today without noticing. It sits underneath Flink’s checkpointed operator state, Kafka Streams’ local state stores, TiKV (the transactional key-value layer that powers TiDB), and a growing family of feature stores that keep precomputed ML features close to model servers. Wherever a system must persist fast-changing state on a single node — high-frequency telemetry ingestion, embeddings stored by key, feature rows joined at inference time — an embedded engine that absorbs writes quickly is the difference between a flat tail-latency graph and a wall of write stalls.

That engine is almost always an LSM tree, not a B-tree. Classical relational engines organize data with B-trees: PostgreSQL’s heap plus B-tree indexes and InnoDB’s clustered index inside MySQL both mutate pages in place, which is excellent for reads but turns every random insert into several page writes. We walked both designs in our PostgreSQL and MySQL server source tours, and SQLite applies the same in-place philosophy to its b-tree layer. An LSM inverts the trade: it accepts writes into an in-memory structure, appends a recovery log for durability, and rewrites data later in bulk sequential passes. For machine-learning workloads — heavy feature updates, training-event ingestion, state written far more often than read — that inversion is exactly what you want.

Here we read facebook/rocksdb at its main branch and trace the lifecycle of one key: from DB::Put through the write-ahead log, the skip-list memtable, a flush into an SST file, background compaction, and the read path that stitches all layers back together. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual tree, and the two diagrams link each node to its source file.

RocksDB at a glance: the write path flows left to right through WAL and memtable into L0 files, while background threads rewrite data downward and every change is published through the manifest-backed VersionSet.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Write admission. DBImpl::Write, L230 is the front door for all mutations; it funnels every writer into WriteImpl, where concurrent writers are grouped under a single leader.
  • Durability first. Writer::AddRecord, L87 frames each batch as a CRC32C-checksummed record in the write-ahead log before anything becomes visible.
  • In-memory ingest. MemTable::Add, L1132 encodes sequence number, type, key, and value into an arena-allocated entry of the active memtable.
  • Flush trigger. FlushJob::Run, L224 streams an immutable memtable into a fresh L0 SST file on the flush thread.
  • SST construction. BlockBasedTableBuilder::Add, L2209 packs entries into compressed data blocks while the builder accumulates index and filter blocks for the final file.
  • Background rewrites. CompactionJob::Run, L1282 merges overlapping runs into lower levels, discarding shadowed and deleted data.
  • Metadata publication. VersionSet::LogAndApply, L6641 is the single serialized point where new file lists are appended to the MANIFEST and swapped in as an immutable Version.
  • Reads. DBImpl::GetImpl, L155 checks live and immutable memtables first, then probes the current Version’s levels newest-first.

The detailed view expands each stage into its concrete functions: leader/follower write batching, the InlineSkipList, BuildTable, bloom filters inside the block-based table format, and the compaction iterator that resolves duplicates and merge operands.

Why a Write-Optimized Engine Matters for ML Workloads

The clearest evidence for the LSM design is who embeds it. Flink offers a RocksDB-backed state backend precisely because windowed aggregations and join buffers update state thousands of times per second, far more than they scan it. Kafka Streams ships RocksDB as its default local store for the same reason. TiKV layered the Raft-replicated transactional protocol on top, and vector-search extensions treat it as a durable index substrate. In each case the pattern repeats: an analytics or serving system needs a per-node, crash-safe, write-heavy cache that survives restarts without the ceremony of running a database server.

The recovery story matters as much as the speed. Because every mutation lands in both the WAL and the memtable, a job that crashes mid-window restarts with its state intact: the engine replays the log, rebuilds the memtable, and serving continues. That property — durable local state without a network round trip per update — is what let stream processors move window aggregation off remote databases. It also reshapes the failure modes: instead of lock contention you watch for write stalls, L0 pileups, and compaction debt, all of which are visible in this source tree rather than hidden behind a query planner.

RocksDB’s answer is to make the expensive work asynchronous. A put pays for one log append plus one in-memory insert, and the reorganization cost is deferred to background threads that batch many updates into sequential file rewrites. That is also why it behaves so differently from a general SQL engine: it deliberately accumulates redundancy across levels and cleans it up later, a bet that wins when writes dominate.

The LSM Idea, in Code

The write path shows the design’s economy. Inside WriteImpl, writers queue up and WriteThread::EnterAsMemTableWriter, L574 elects one leader that will write the WAL and install memtable entries on behalf of the whole group — turning N concurrent writers into one sequential append. DBImpl::WriteToWAL, L2330 merges the group into a single batch. Once the record is durable, WriteBatchInternal::InsertInto, L3296 replays the serialized batch, and the MemTableInserter, L2045 handler translates each Put/Delete/Merge record into memtable calls.

The memtable itself is a probabilistic skip list rather than a balanced tree. SkipListRep::Insert, L42 forwards into InlineSkipList::Insert, L103, a lock-free structure where concurrent inserts and reads never block each other — one reason RocksDB can saturate multi-core writers without latching the memtable. Because the list is kept sorted, the later flush is a simple merge pass, not a re-sort.

Flush and the SST File Format

When the active memtable fills, the flush thread takes over. DBImpl::BackgroundCallFlush, L4999 loops forever picking work, and MemTableList::PickMemtablesToFlush, L495 selects the oldest immutable memtables. DBImpl::FlushMemTableToOutputFile, L191 builds the job, and BuildTable, L74 — shared with compaction — turns an iterator stream into one sorted file.

The file format is where reads stay fast. BlockBasedTableBuilder::Finish, L4018 emits the index blocks, metadata, and footer after the data blocks are written. Alongside, FullFilterBlockBuilder::Add, L67 accumulates bloom/Ribbon bits for every key prefix, so a point lookup can reject a whole file with one hash probe. On the read side, BlockBasedTable::Open, L738 loads footer and index into memory, and the per-SST lookup defined in BlockBasedTable::Get, L509 consults the filter before fetching a single data block.

Compaction: Paying Down Write Debt

Compaction is the LSM’s garbage collector. DBImpl::BackgroundCallCompaction, L5100 drives the loop, and LevelCompactionPicker::PickCompaction, L1000 chooses a level plus overlapping inputs using score-based heuristics. CompactionJob::Run, L1282 then merges those runs through CompactionIterator::NextFromInput, L1012, the heart of the engine: it deduplicates sequence numbers, respects snapshots, drops tombstones once they reach the bottom level, and applies compaction filters. User-defined merges are resolved by MergeHelper::MergeUntil, L281 using whatever MergeOperator the application supplied.

Every rewrite ends at VersionSet::LogAndApply, L6641 — flushes and compactions both publish through it, which is why readers never see a half-installed file list. Applications can also force the process with DB::CompactRange at DBImpl::CompactRange, L1192, useful before long-lived range scans or after bulk loads.

Leveled is only the default style. The same directory carries a universal picker for write-heavy workloads that prefer many small overlapping runs, and a FIFO picker that simply drops data once a size or TTL threshold passes — compaction_picker_universal.cc and compaction_picker_fifo.cc sit beside compaction_picker_level.cc in the tree. All of them feed the same CompactionJob machinery, so a column family can switch styles through options without touching the rest of the engine.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository’s INSTALL.md keeps the build deliberately simple. The library compiles with C++20 and needs GCC 11 or newer (or Clang 10 or newer) per INSTALL.md L9. The recommended target is make static_lib, producing librocksdb.a in release mode (INSTALL.md L13); make shared_lib builds the shared variant instead. If the binary must run on older CPUs, set PORTABLE=1 (INSTALL.md L25). Compression libraries — zlib, bzip2, lz4, snappy, zstandard — are optional link-time accelerators (INSTALL.md L35), and only the tools need gflags; the library builds without it.

Your first program is thirty lines. The public surface starts at DB::Open, L289, and examples/simple_example.cc shows the canonical skeleton: open at DB::Open(options, kDBPath, &db), L38, then write at db->Put, L42. To turn this into a feature-store skeleton, define a column family per feature group via ColumnFamilyOptions, batch feature-row upserts into one WriteBatch per inference request, and set bloom filters on — the filter block you saw in the format section is what keeps point lookups at a handful of comparisons.

Honest Limits

  • It is a library, not a database. The README states plainly that “this code is a library that forms the core building block for a fast key-value server” (README.md L7). There is no SQL layer, no network protocol, and no replication scheme included — systems like TiKV build those on top.
  • Read amplification is real. The project itself advertises tradeoffs between write-, read-, and space-amplification factors (README.md L9). A cold Get may probe the memtable, immutable memtables, and one file per level; the bloom filter bounds, but does not eliminate, that cost.
  • Tuning is a discipline. DBOptions and ColumnFamilyOptions in options.h L601 expose hundreds of knobs, and the repository carries a DEFAULT_OPTIONS_HISTORY.md to track how defaults changed across releases — a hint about how much behavior depends on them.
  • Build defaults can mislead. INSTALL.md warns in its first lines that plain make compiles debug-mode binaries that are “much slower than release mode” (INSTALL.md L3); benchmarks built from default targets will undersell the engine.

An LSM engine is a wager that the future rewrites what you wrote yesterday. RocksDB implements that wager with unusual rigor — a lock-free memtable, crash-safe group commit, immutable SSTs, and a versioned manifest — which is why so much of the AI infrastructure stack, from stream processors to feature stores, keeps choosing it as the last write stop before disk.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of facebook/rocksdb, the LSM-tree storage engine embedded in TiKV, Flink, and Kafka Streams, tracing the write path, skip-list memtable, SST files, and background compaction through verified code anchors.

entry.title: SQLite Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the World’s Most Deployed Database

link.title: SQLite Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the World’s Most Deployed Database

entry.content:
SQLite is almost certainly running within arm’s reach of you right now. It is the database inside every phone, every major browser, most operating systems, and an enormous share of embedded devices. It has no server process, no network protocol, and no configuration file — it is a C library that links into your application and owns a single file on disk. That design is exactly why the AI world keeps adopting it: edge inference boxes, local-first desktop apps, and on-device retrieval all need structured state without operating a database cluster.

The AI connection has become concrete. Embedding-heavy applications increasingly treat SQLite as a local vector store — the popular sqlite-vec extension follows in the footsteps of the in-tree vec1 ANN extension that now lives in ext/vec1/, and full-text retrieval has shipped in the core tree for years as FTS5. When you build on-device RAG, an agent’s memory store, or a local-first annotation layer for model outputs, you are deploying this codebase. Understanding its internals therefore pays off in the same way our tours of (PostgreSQL) and (MySQL) did: the storage layer you depend on stops being a black box.

In this tour we read the sqlite/sqlite GitHub mirror of the canonical Fossil repository (version 3.55.0 at the time of writing). Two diagrams anchor the walk: a compact overview of the layer stack, and a detailed graph of the compile path and the write path with real function names and line numbers.

Layer view of SQLite. Statements enter through the public API, are compiled to a VDBE program, and execute down through B-tree, pager, and WAL into the pluggable VFS.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Client entry — sqlite3_exec, L30 is the classic one-shot helper: it prepares each statement and steps it to completion. Connections themselves are created by sqlite3_open_v2, L3768, which allocates the handle and attaches one B-tree per database file.
  • Compile — sqlite3_prepare_v2, L972 compiles one SQL string into a virtual-machine program.
  • Tokenize — sqlite3RunParser, L600 walks the text, classifies tokens, and drives the parser.
  • Grammar — sqlite3Parser, L59 is a Lemon LALR(1) grammar, not hand-written C; tool/lemon.c generates parse.c from it at build time.
  • Plan and emit — sqlite3WhereBegin, L6954 is the query planner: it picks indexes and join orders and emits the loop opcodes.
  • Execute — sqlite3VdbeExec, L903 is the register-based virtual machine — one giant switch over opcodes.
  • Store — sqlite3BtreeBeginTrans, L3838 opens transactions on the B-tree, and sqlite3PagerSharedLock, L5323 is where journaling and locking begin.
  • Durability — in WAL mode the pager hands frames to sqlite3WalFrames, L4376; everything ultimately lands on disk through the VFS, e.g. unixRead, L3512.

Detailed graph: the compile path from tokens to opcodes on top, the storage stack from B-tree cells to VFS writes below, with the WAL branch on the side.

From Install to Your First Model

Building SQLite from this repository is deliberately boring — that is part of its engineering culture. On Unix, the README prescribes: install gcc make tcl-dev, unpack the tree, create a build directory, then run ../sqlite/configure followed by make sqlite3 for the command-line shell and make sqlite3.c for the amalgamation. Core deliverables build without TCL; TCL is only needed for the test targets. On Windows the tree ships a make.bat so make sqlite3.exe works under MSVC, or you can call nmake /f Makefile.msc directly.

The amalgamation deserves a moment. make sqlite3.c runs Tcl scripts that stitch every source and header into one enormous translation unit — over 200K lines. Compile-time cross-procedure analysis across that single file makes the engine about 5% faster than building from separate objects, which is why every language binding embeds the amalgamation rather than the tree.

Now your “first model” — in the AI sense, a table of embeddings. The tree contains ext/vec1/vec1.c, an ANN vector extension (version 0.8) whose header documents an AVX2 loadable build: gcc -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx2 -mfma vec1.c -shared -fPIC -o vec1.so. Load it through the standard extension entry sqlite3_extension_init, L13145; it exposes L2 and cosine distance metrics (constants at L26) and reports itself with SELECT vec1_info(). For keyword recall, FTS5 ships in-tree and initializes via sqlite3Fts5Init, L3906. A hybrid store — FTS5 for lexical, vec1 for dense, plus your own metadata columns — fits comfortably in one file, which is precisely the local-RAG shape many apps want before graduating to a dedicated server like (Qdrant).

The Compile Path: SQL Text to a VM Program

Compilation starts in sqlite3Prepare, L717, a driver that resolves schemas and retries if the schema version changes underneath it. It hands the SQL text to sqlite3RunParser, L600, whose inner loop calls a token classifier and then the Lemon-generated parser. The grammar file src/parse.y carries the %name sqlite3Parser directive; each grammar action either builds AST objects (Expr, Select, Table) or calls code generators directly.

DDL flows through sqlite3StartTable, L1292, which allocates the Table object and root pages, and sqlite3EndTable, L2757, which writes the schema row and emits OP_ParseSchema. Queries flow through sqlite3Select, L7807, the top-level SELECT compiler. Expressions funnel into sqlite3ExprCodeTarget, L5110, which turns an expression tree into opcodes that leave results in registers. The planner call from select.c is sqlite3WhereBegin, L6954; when it returns, the join loops are coded, and sqlite3WhereEnd, L7657 closes them and frees the plan. Every emitted instruction lands through sqlite3VdbeAddOp3, L274, and sqlite3VdbeMakeReady, L2664 finalizes the program frame.

Inside the VDBE

SQLite’s execution model is a bytecode interpreter, not a tree-walker — a choice that gives it deterministic, steppable execution: sqlite3_step() runs the program until the next row is ready. The public stepping entry is sqlite3_step, L990, and the interpreter core is sqlite3VdbeExec, L903. Even the opcode list itself is generated: a Tcl script scans src/vdbe.c to produce opcodes.h and opcodes.c (the README documents this). When a statement finishes, sqlite3VdbeHalt, L3348 decides whether to commit, roll back, or just release cursors. EXPLAIN simply prints this program, so every statement you run has a fully visible assembly listing — an excellent debugging surface for AI agents that generate SQL at runtime.

The Storage Stack: B-Tree, Pager, WAL

Below the VM sits the classic three-layer stack. The B-tree layer (sqlite3BtreeOpen, L2565) manages pages, cursors, and balancing: sqlite3BtreeCursor, L4802 positions a cursor, accessPayload, L5158 decodes record bytes including overflow pages, and sqlite3BtreeInsert, L9445 writes cells and rebalances. Transactions open at sqlite3BtreeBeginTrans, L3838 and commit at sqlite3BtreeCommit, L4467.

The pager (sqlite3PagerSharedLock, L5323) owns locking, journaling, and the page cache. Page fetches enter at sqlite3PagerGet, L5795 (its worker getPageNormal at L5604 resolves reads from the WAL when needed). Commits split into two phases — sqlite3PagerCommitPhaseOne, L6534 and sqlite3PagerCommitPhaseTwo, L6771 — and choose a durability route: the rollback-journal path journals pages first and rewrites them through pager_write_pagelist, L4490, while the WAL path appends frames instead (the call site for sqlite3WalFrames sits at pager.c:3280).

The WAL branch is worth studying on its own. After a crash, walIndexRecover, L1422 rebuilds the wal-index from the log; readers binary-search it with sqlite3WalFindFrame, L3737 and copy page images via sqlite3WalReadFrame, L3755; writers serialize through the write lock at sqlite3WalBeginWriteTransaction, L3800. Because every I/O goes through the pluggable VFS dispatch (sqlite3OsWrite, L92 into unixWrite, L3643), the whole engine ports to exotic filesystems by implementing one small interface — the same trick that lets the vector and FTS extensions live in one file with your metadata.

SQLite in the AI Data Layer

Why should an AI engineer care? Because the modern stack keeps rediscovering that most intelligence workloads start small and local. Prototypes store embeddings next to the app that computes them; agents keep session state and tool results in a file; edge devices log inferences where the network is not guaranteed. SQLite’s zero-administration design means the “database deployment” is a linked library and a filename. Compared with embedded analytical engines like (DuckDB) — which we tour separately — SQLite optimizes for transactional durability and tiny footprint rather than columnar scans, and the two compose well in the same process. And when a local store outgrows one machine, the migration path to server systems like (Qdrant) for vectors or (PostgreSQL) for general workloads is straightforward because the data model is plain SQL. Allocation is centralized too: everything from VM registers to page-cache frames flows through sqlite3_malloc64, L322, so memory profiling a local RAG service has a single choke point. Even authorization is pluggable at the compile step via sqlite3_set_authorizer, L70, which multi-tenant tooling can use to gate which statements an LLM is allowed to run.

Honest Limits

SQLite is not a client/server database, and the source makes that unmistakable: there is no network listener anywhere in the tree — the “client” is a function call and the storage backends are file VFS implementations. Concurrency is bounded: WAL mode permits one writer at a time, enforced by the single WAL write lock, and cross-process coordination relies on file locking rather than a broker. There are no server-side user accounts; access control is whatever the host process enforces through the authorizer callback. The engine also carries real complexity — the README itself warns that the amalgamation exceeds 200K lines, chokes some symbolic debuggers, and that it “will not be the easiest library in the world to hack.” None of this diminishes its role; it defines it. For the AI data layer, SQLite is the floor of the pyramid — the substrate on which (MySQL) and the server engines above it were eventually needed.
entry.summary: A source tour of the sqlite/sqlite repository showing how the tokenizer, Lemon parser, VDBE virtual machine, B-tree, pager, WAL, and VFS layers turn SQL text into durable pages.

entry.title: TiDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the MySQL-Compatible Distributed SQL Layer

link.title: TiDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the MySQL-Compatible Distributed SQL Layer

entry.content:
Every ML platform eventually hits the same wall: the feature store, the event log, or the experiment tracker outgrows a single MySQL instance, and the team is forced to choose between sharding by hand and rewriting the app for some exotic store. TiDB is the escape hatch that keeps the MySQL dialect. It is an open-source distributed SQL database, written in Go, that speaks the MySQL 8.0 protocol on the wire while spreading rows across a cluster of TiKV storage nodes with Raft replication and distributed two-phase-commit transactions. Because the protocol, drivers, and most of the SQL surface stay the same, a Python training job or a FastAPI backend that used pymysql against MySQL keeps working against TiDB with a connection-string change.

The second reason TiDB matters to AI infrastructure is HTAP. TiDB can replicate the same data into TiFlash, a columnar storage engine, using the Multi-Raft Learner protocol, so analytical scans over event tables and features run against column replicas without stealing CPU from the transactional path. For ML workloads that is a clean split: point reads and writes for serving, columnar aggregates for training-set extraction, drift monitoring, and cohort analysis, all inside one system. The README frames it exactly this way: TiFlash “uses the Multi-Raft Learner protocol to replicate data from TiKV in real time” while the TiDB layer “coordinates query execution across both TiKV and TiFlash”.

The third reason is architectural clarity. TiDB separates stateless compute from storage: the pingcap/tidb repository you clone contains only the SQL layer — the MySQL frontend, the planner, the executors — while persistence lives in TiKV (backed by an LSM tree, the same family as RocksDB) and placement metadata lives in PD. The compute layer is just a Go binary you can scale horizontally, which maps neatly onto cloud AI stacks where stateless services and replicated storage are managed independently — spin up more SQL nodes for a burst of concurrent notebooks, or more TiKV nodes as the feature store grows, and neither operation touches the other. This post tours that compute layer in source, tracing one SELECT from packet to row batch. If you want the same treatment for a shared-nothing peer, see the CockroachDB tour.

Overview: one query's path through the TiDB compute layer — MySQL protocol in, executor tree in the middle, region-scoped coprocessor RPCs to TiKV at the bottom, with the commit path closing the loop back to the session.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Every accepted socket becomes a session at Server.Run, L506, which passes each connection to newConn, L294 to be paired with a TiDBContext.
  • The packet loop lives in clientConn.Run, L1157 — this is the MySQL wire dialect, not gRPC, which is what makes existing MySQL tooling drop-in compatible.
  • Command routing happens in dispatch, L1444, and a COM_QUERY lands in handleQuery, L1864 with the raw SQL text.
  • The session entry point is session.ExecuteStmt, L2489, which coordinates parse, plan, execute, and the eventual autocommit.
  • Planning starts at Optimize, L148, which checks the plan cache before paying for a fresh optimization.
  • The physical plan becomes an executor tree in build, L195, and rows are pulled up through Next, L63 — a volcano model, but tree leaves can be remote.
  • Remote leaves ship their scans through distsql.Select, L62, which drives region-scoped work in copIterator.Next, L1441.
  • Writes end at doCommitWithRetry, L817, which pushes the transaction into TiKV’s two-phase commit protocol and retries on conflict.

Detail: the same flow expanded into verified functions — dispatch, ExecStmt, Optimize, buildSelect, findBestTask, the executor zoo, RequestBuilder, buildCopTasks, and the kv interfaces every backend implements.

The MySQL Wire: One Binary That Speaks 8.0

The pkg/server package is a complete MySQL protocol implementation: handshake, auth plugins (including caching SHA-2 and even SM3), command dispatch, prepared statements, and result encoders. clientConn.Run, L1157 is a loop that reads frames and hands each to dispatch, L1444, a switch over command bytes. Text queries reach handleQuery, L1864; binary protocol prepared statements have their own file. The adapter that bridges protocol and engine is ExecStmt in pkg/executor/adapter.go, L392: its Exec method at L656 orchestrates planning and execution, while buildExecutor at L1592 turns the finished plan into runnable operators. Compared with the classic single-node tree in MySQL Server, the remarkable part is that none of this code knows it is talking to a cluster.

Planner: From AST to a Priced Physical Plan

Planning begins when the session calls ExecuteStmt and lands in Optimize, L148. TiDB first consults the non-prepared plan cache — a big win for dashboards and scheduled feature queries that re-run the same shapes every few minutes — then builds a logical plan. PlanBuilder.Build at pkg/planner/core/planbuilder.go, L601 is the giant dispatcher: SELECT statements go to buildSelect at logical_plan_builder.go, L4349, which lowers joins, filters, and aggregates into a logical tree. The cost-based step is findBestTask at find_best_task.go, L604: for a data source it enumerates access paths — TableReader, IndexReader, IndexLookUp — and prices them using table statistics. Those statistics come from Histogram at statistics/histogram.go, L65, a bucketed column sketch collected by ANALYZE. This is the same planner philosophy you find in Postgres — estimates decide shapes — but here the winner may be a plan fragment that runs on storage nodes or on TiFlash.

Executors and the DistSQL Round Trip

Everything below the planner is a tree of pull-based operators. The contract is tiny: Executor at pkg/executor/internal/exec/executor.go, L51 requires Next at L63 that fills a columnar chunk. Point lookups skip the machinery entirely: PointGetExecutor at point_get.go, L118 fetches one key straight from the transaction buffer — the path your key-value-style feature lookups should take. Full scans use TableReaderExecutor at table_reader.go, L139 or IndexReaderExecutor at distsql.go, L222; the latter’s sibling IndexLookUpExecutor at L502 double-reads index handles then rows. When a leaf cannot be served locally, the builder emits a DistSQL scan: RequestBuilder.Build, L61 packs the key ranges (SetHandleRanges, L156) and a serialized DAG of operators (SetDAGRequest, L203) into a kv.Request. Note what is being pushed down: the filter and projection logic ships to the data, and ProjectionExec at projection.go, L77 only handles what remains.

TiKV, TiFlash, and Two-Phase Commit

The storage half of the story lives behind interfaces in pkg/kv: Transaction at kv/kv.go, L264, Snapshot at L815, and Storage at L867. The production implementation is a driver over tikv/client-go: tikvStore at store/driver/tikv_driver.go, L327 and tikvTxn at store/driver/txn/txn_driver.go, L47. Reads fan out through pkg/store/copr: buildCopTasks at coprocessor.go, L529 cuts key ranges by region cache, and copIterator at L990 runs the per-region requests with bounded concurrency. Each task reads a consistent snapshot of its region, so a scan spanning thousands of regions still sees one point-in-time version of your table — the property that makes a training-set extraction reproducible while serving traffic mutates the rows underneath. Analytical plans instead route through MPPClient at mpp.go, L46, which coordinates fragments pushed to TiFlash columnar replicas. Writes end in the famous protocol: the session’s doCommit at session.go, L540 stages the write set, and doCommitWithRetry at L817 drives the client-go committer through prewrite and commit phases with retry on lock conflict. Underneath it all, TiKV persists to an LSM engine in the same family as RocksDB, with Raft keeping replicas consistent.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s Quick Start is deliberately infrastructure-shaped, and it matters here that this repository alone is only the SQL layer — a working cluster also needs TiKV and PD nodes, which the tooling below provisions for you:

  1. Start a cluster. For a local test playground, follow the official quick start guide (the README links docs.pingcap.com → quick-start-with-tidb → deploy a local test cluster), which uses TiUP to launch TiDB, TiKV, and PD processes on one machine. For Kubernetes, the README points to TiDB Operator. For a managed cluster with a free tier, the README recommends TiDB Cloud.
  2. Connect with a MySQL client or driver. Because the wire protocol is MySQL 8.0 compatible, mysql CLI, SQLAlchemy, pymysql, or any Go/Java/Python MySQL driver works unmodified — the README’s step 3 is literally “Use a MySQL driver or an ORM”.
  3. Create a schema and load feature rows. Standard DDL and DML: CREATE TABLE, bulk INSERT, and LOAD DATA-style ingestion paths.
  4. Read analytics from the same cluster. Once a table has TiFlash replicas, aggregate queries can be served columnar — the README’s feature list calls this HTAP and notes the TiDB server “coordinates query execution across both TiKV and TiFlash”.

For a real training workflow the practical first milestone is: point your existing SQLAlchemy connection string at the TiDB endpoint, run your migration scripts unchanged, and only then start thinking about replicas and TiFlash.

Honest Limits

  • This repo is not a database you can run alone. Cloned and built, pingcap/tidb gives you the SQL compute layer; without TiKV and PD endpoints it cannot serve queries. The full topology is a distributed system to operate — PD placement, region balance, replica counts — not a single binary.
  • MySQL compatibility is broad, not total. The README says “compatible with MySQL 8.0” and points to a dedicated compatibility doc; some MySQL features behave differently or are unsupported, so run your real workload’s SQL against a test cluster before migrating.
  • The codebase is huge and moves fast. The Go module spans thousands of packages across pkg/executor, pkg/planner, pkg/store, plus the br, dumpling, and lightning tool trees; anchors in this post were verified against master and will drift.
  • The trickiest logic is partly elsewhere. The two-phase committer and region routing live in the tikv/client-go dependency, so reading this repo alone does not show the full commit path — you must follow it across the module boundary.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of pingcap/tidb, following one query from the MySQL wire protocol through the cost-based planner, volcano executors and DistSQL down to the TiKV coprocessor and two-phase commit.

entry.title: cuDF: Inside NVIDIA’s GPU DataFrame Engine That Speaks Fluent pandas

link.title: cuDF: Inside NVIDIA’s GPU DataFrame Engine That Speaks Fluent pandas

entry.content:
Every serious ML workflow eventually hits the same wall: the model trains on the GPU, but the data prep before it runs on the CPU. Feature engineering, joins, group-by aggregations, CSV and Parquet parsing — all of it grinds through single-threaded pandas while an expensive accelerator sits idle. cuDF, part of NVIDIA’s RAPIDS ecosystem, attacks exactly that gap. It gives you a DataFrame API that mirrors pandas almost one-to-one, but every column lives in GPU device memory and every operation compiles down to CUDA kernels. The result is not a toy: the README points at production consumers ranging from the NVIDIA Spark plugin to Velox-based query engines, which use cuDF’s column primitives as their execution substrate.

The repo itself is layered like an onion, and that layering is what makes it interesting to read. At the top sits the cudf Python package with its familiar DataFrame and Series. Beneath it, pylibcudf exposes Cython bindings over libcudf, a CUDA C++ library with Apache Arrow-compliant data structures. The README also documents cudf.pandas for zero-code-change acceleration of existing pandas scripts, cudf-polars as a GPU engine for Polars, and dask-cudf for scaling across many GPUs. Because the pieces are cleanly separated, you can trace one pandas call from the comfort of Python all the way down to a raw device buffer.

This post walks that path with two maps. The overview shows the vertical story — Python API, Cython bridge, C++ core, IO, GPU memory — and the detail diagram digs into columns, views, null masks, aggregations, joins, and the Parquet reader machinery.

The cuDF stack: a pandas-shaped Python surface on top of the pylibcudf Cython bindings, which drive the libcudf C++ core and its GPU-backed readers.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at DataFrame, L991, the pandas-mirroring class users actually touch. It holds its data through a column accessor and only lowers to pylibcudf when an operation actually needs kernels.
  • GroupBy, L541 collects pandas-style split/apply/combine requests before shipping them across the bridge as a batch.
  • IO entry points like read_parquet, L944 import pylibcudf directly and hand file paths to the readers below.
  • The bridge is built from small Cython classes: Table, L68 and Column, L329 wrap the C++ containers one-to-one.
  • pylibcudf’s GroupBy, L98 and its Parquet bindings in io/parquet.pyx, L794 are thin enough that the C++ signatures stay visible.
  • The C++ core types are deliberately boring: cudf::table, L31 is just an ordered set of columns, and cudf::column, L37 is device data plus a validity mask.
  • cudf::groupby, L90 does the heavy lifting — grouping keys by hash or sort, then computing requested aggregations.
  • On the IO side, cudf::io::read_parquet, L1027 decodes Parquet column chunks straight into GPU tables.
  • Finally, gpumemoryview, L83 gives Python zero-copy views over the RMM device allocations that back every column.

Internals: how the Python column objects, the Cython layer, the C++ core types, the operation kernels, and the GPU runtime fit together.

Three Libraries, One Column Model

The genius of the design is that there is only one data model, and it is Arrow-flavored. A cudf::column owns a device buffer of typed values plus a validity bitmask; a cudf::table owns an ordered set of columns. Everything above that is a view or a binding. Python’s ColumnBase, L674 mirrors the C++ column, and the ColumnAccessor, L113 maps column names to those objects so DataFrame can behave like a dictionary of columns.

Because C++ algorithms should never mutate inputs they don’t own, the library is strict about ownership. cudf::column_view, L317 and cudf::table_view, L206 are non-owning projections that get passed into every kernel-facing API. This zero-copy discipline means a slice, a join probe, or a sort key costs nothing to hand off. Scalars get the same treatment: cudf::scalar, L45 is a device-side single value with numeric and string specializations, so fill values and literal operands never round-trip through host memory.

Groupby, Joins, and Sorting on the GPU

The operation layer reads like a distributed-systems toolkit compressed into one header directory. Grouped aggregation starts from cudf::groupby, L90, which accepts aggregation_request lists pairing keys with operations. The operations themselves are typed by aggregation::Kind, L76 — SUM, MEAN, and friends — one vocabulary shared by groupby, reductions, and rolling windows.

Joins come in several flavors, with cudf::hash_join, L61 as the workhorse: build a hash table on one key table, probe it with the other, all over table_view inputs. The hash functions are exposed too — murmurhash3_x86_32, L58 alongside MD5 and SHA variants — which matters for sharding and fingerprinting. Sorting is expressed as index computation: sorted_order, L44 returns the gather indices that put rows in order, and the Python sort_values, L3750 method simply applies the resulting permutation. Even null handling is a first-class operation set: bitmask_and, L224 and its siblings combine validity masks whenever two columns with nulls meet.

How a Parquet File Becomes a GPU Table

Parquet is the format most ML datasets ship in, so its reader is worth tracing explicitly. The C++ entry point read_parquet, L1027 accepts a settings object — parquet_reader_options, L70, assembled through a builder that takes a source, column selections, and predicate pushdown filters — and returns a table_with_metadata, with columns already resident on the device. The construction of the actual reader is visible in reader::reader, L12, where generic data sources become the internal state the decoding implementation consumes. Below that sit the page-decoding kernels under cpp/src/io/parquet — RLE streams, delta encodings, and page header parsers — that turn compressed column chunks into typed device buffers without ever staging the bytes on the host. Predicate pushdown happens early: statistics are consulted so entire row groups can be skipped before any GPU work is spent on them.

Streams shape the rest of the runtime contract. Nearly every pylibcudf function takes an optional stream parameter typed as CudaStreamLike, L15, an alias accepting an RMM Stream, any object exposing the CUDA stream protocol, or a raw cudaStream_t. That makes every operation stream-ordered: kernel launches land on the caller’s stream, so a training loop can overlap data prep on one stream with model compute on another. Inside libcudf, cuda_stream_pool, L26 hands out pooled streams to operations that want concurrency without paying stream-creation cost each time. Memory and streams together explain why cuDF feels synchronous while staying asynchronous underneath — the API returns once work is ordered on your stream, not necessarily once the GPU has finished executing it.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s installation section is refreshingly direct. From PyPI you pick the wheel matching your CUDA major version — the -cu## suffix is mandatory matching, not a suggestion:

pip install cudf-cu12

Conda users get the same thing from the RAPIDS channel:

conda install -c rapidsai cudf

Then the API really is pandas-shaped. The README’s own example reads Parquet and aggregates in two lines:

import cudf

df = cudf.read_parquet("data.parquet")
df.dropna().groupby(["A", "B"]).mean()

If you already have pandas code, you don’t change it — you run it through the accelerator: python -m cudf.pandas script.py, or in a notebook call %load_ext cudf.pandas before importing pandas. The proxy machinery in _FastSlowProxy, L816 dispatches each operation to a fast GPU implementation when possible and falls back to the real pandas otherwise. Polars users get a different door: build a lazy frame and call collect(engine="gpu"), which routes execution through cudf-polars.

For ML engineers the payoff shows up right where training starts. A typical flow — load a Parquet dataset, drop nulls, group-and-aggregate to build features, then hand the tensors to your trainer — keeps every step on the device instead of shuttling arrays through host memory. The same trick applies to text preprocessing before tokenization: cuDF ships string kernels built on strings_column_view, L27, plus tokenizer vocabularies and wordpiece modules in its core package. And because the operation vocabulary covers sorting, dedup, and binary operations like binary_operation, L172, most feature-transform code that would have been a dozen pandas calls becomes the same dozen calls, each one executing as a kernel.

Honest Limits

The README is honest about the contract, and so should you be. The Python API “mirrors” pandas, and the README itself says the APIs are largely similar — not identical. Code that leans on obscure pandas corners or third-party extension types may still need adjustments, and cudf.pandas exists precisely because the two implementations are not interchangeable at every call site.

Version matching is another hard requirement: the PyPI wheels use a -cu12 or -cu13 suffix, and you must match the major version of your installed CUDA toolkit. System requirements — operating system, GPU driver, supported CUDA versions — live in NVIDIA’s separate install docs rather than being baked into the pip install. Memory is physical, too: columns live in device memory, so dataset size is bounded by your GPU’s VRAM unless you scale out with dask-cudf across devices. And while the Parquet, CSV, and JSON readers cover the common formats, exotic sources will still need a conversion step before they become GPU columns. None of these are dealbreakers — they are the edges of a very large, very fast island.

Where cuDF Fits in the Wider Data Stack

cuDF does not try to replace every system; it plugs into them. The README lists an Apache Spark GPU plugin, a Velox extension that executes query engine plans on the GPU, and integration points with SQL engines. The Polars connection is the most developer-visible one, since cudf-polars makes a mature query planner run against GPU columns. For multi-GPU or multi-node datasets, Dask provides the scaling story via dask-cudf. The Arrow-compliant memory layout is what makes these handoffs cheap, echoing the same zero-copy philosophy as Arrow itself. And if your feature engineering feeds a training job whose inference path runs through Spark, the same column model appears on both sides of the wall.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of rapidsai/cudf — the pandas-like Python API, the pylibcudf Cython bridge, and the libcudf C++/CUDA kernels that turn DataFrames into GPU column operations.

entry.title: DataFusion: The Rust and Arrow Query Engine Powering Embeddable Analytics

link.title: DataFusion: The Rust and Arrow Query Engine Powering Embeddable Analytics

entry.content:
Modern AI and ML work is, more often than we admit, query-shaped. Before a model sees a tensor, somebody filters events, joins features, aggregates sessions, and dedupes rows out of a lake of Parquet files. Enter Apache DataFusion: an extensible query engine written in Rust that uses Apache Arrow as its in-memory format. It is not a database you install but a library you link into your own application.

For AI data infrastructure, that design pays off three ways. Feature preparation is Parquet-centric, and DataFusion treats Parquet, CSV, JSON, and Avro as first-class inputs. A DataFrame API means analytics code can feed model training without a detour through a separate warehouse. And because the engine is embeddable, your data app and your query engine are one process - no socket hop, no serialization boundary. Subprojects extend the reach: DataFusion Python adds a Python interface for SQL and DataFrame queries, Comet accelerates Apache Spark, and Ballista scales execution across a cluster.

This post is a source tour, not a marketing page: everything below was read from the repository’s main branch, and both diagrams were compiled from the real file tree. Figure 1 shows a query’s path; Figure 2 digs into sessions, rules, streams, and spills.

Figure 1 - A query's end-to-end flow, from SQL text or DataFrame calls to Parquet scans emitting Arrow batches.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • You start at SessionContext, L281, the front door owning shared session state; its sql() method, L612 takes SQL text, while the DataFrame, L220 wraps the same machinery for programmatic use.
  • SQL text first hits DFParser, L439, extending standard SQL with DataFusion DDL such as CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE; the entry point is parse_sql, L593.
  • The AST is lowered by SqlToRel, L442, which resolves tables against a ContextProvider; the dispatcher is statement_to_plan, L221.
  • The result is a LogicalPlan, L267 - an immutable relational-algebra tree. The DataFrame API builds identical trees via LogicalPlanBuilder, L208, and every predicate is a typed Expr, L314.
  • Optimization runs inside SessionState::optimize, L781: analyzer first, then logical rules. SessionState, L133 is deliberately scoped to a single query.
  • The optimized plan is compiled by DefaultPhysicalPlanner, L165 into a tree of ExecutionPlan, L89 operators; execute(), L683 returns one Arrow RecordBatch stream per partition.
  • On the data side, ParquetSource, L282 performs scans with row-group pruning and predicate pushdown, and ListingTableFactory, L30 turns object-store paths into partitioned tables.

Figure 2 - The internals: sessions, SQL planning, rule-based rewrites, streaming executors, and the spill machinery.

Why Rust and Arrow Matter for ML Data

The columnar memory model is the quiet hero. Arrow’s RecordBatch is the engine’s currency: scans produce it, executors consume and emit it, nothing in between re-encodes it. If you train on numeric feature tables, that is exactly your layout - columns of primitives ready for vectorized math. We covered the format in our Arrow tour; DataFusion is arguably its most complete pure consumer.

Streaming matters too. execute() returns an async stream per partition, and spawn_buffered, L173 pushes those streams onto tokio tasks with bounded buffers, so a slow consumer cannot force unbounded buffering. Scanning billions of rows to emit one small aggregate keeps memory tracking the working set, not the table size.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest poke is the CLI, a small utility that runs SQL on the engine. The official guide gives two commands: cargo install datafusion-cli, or on macOS brew install datafusion. In the shell, CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE points at a Parquet directory and aggregation starts in seconds.

For a real application, take the crate route, verbatim from the project’s example-usage guide:

datafusion = "55.1.0"
tokio = { version = "1.0", features = ["rt-multi-thread"] }

A first SQL query over CSV, from the same docs:

let ctx = SessionContext::new();
ctx.register_csv("example", "tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new()).await?;
let df = ctx.sql("SELECT a, MIN(b) FROM example WHERE a <= b GROUP BY a LIMIT 100").await?;
df.show().await?;

The identical job with the DataFrame API:

let df = ctx.read_csv("tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new()).await?;
let df = df.filter(col("a").lt_eq(col("b")))?
    .aggregate(vec![col("a")], vec![min(col("b"))])?
    .limit(0, Some(100))?;
df.show().await?;

For a feature-preparation job only the last step changes: call collect(), L1734 and you get Vec<RecordBatch> - Arrow memory ready for a training loader or serialization. Prefer Python? The separate DataFusion Python project offers the same SQL and DataFrame interface. The engine will not train your model; it fetches exactly the rows your model deserves, fast.

Fifty Rules, All in the Open

DataFusion’s performance story is mostly a rule story - and the rules are documented inside the source tree. optimizer_rule_reference.md pins the catalog: 2 analyzer rules, 27 logical rules, and 21 physical rules, in the same order EXPLAIN VERBOSE prints them. The analyzer’s type_coercion rule, L21 inserts implicit casts so every operator receives valid input types. On the logical side, push_down_filter, L45 moves predicates as early as possible, while optimize_projections, L52 prunes columns nobody reads.

Physical planning picks shapes and operators. The join_selection rule, L70 chooses join implementation, build side, and partition mode from statistics, and EnsureRequirements, L74 inserts the repartition and sort nodes each executor requires. A consistency test in optimizer_rule_reference.rs, L41 even fails CI if documented rule order drifts.

Memory, Sort and Spill When Data Outgrows RAM

Embedded engines cannot reserve a warehouse-sized box, so memory discipline is engineered in. SortExec, L1306 states the contract in its header: buffer sorted batches in memory, spill to disk at the limit, merge all runs once input is exhausted. Writing is centralized in SpillManager, L27, which encodes batches as Arrow IPC files and, on replay, wraps the decoded stream in a buffered tokio task.

Aggregation takes the same route: AggregateExec, L863 runs in partial and final modes, and its spill module lets intermediate group tables hit disk. There’s even a streaming join - SymmetricHashJoinExec, L163 - which emits matches as both inputs arrive instead of waiting for a full build side. And for bounded asks like “top 100 per group”, TopK, L100 keeps a small priority queue instead of sorting the world. This is what lets a laptop-sized process crunch a disk-sized table.

Next to DuckDB, Polars and Dask

DuckDB is the closest philosophical neighbor - another in-process analytical engine - but C++ with a server-style SQL shell; DataFusion is Rust, streaming-native, and customizable at almost every point: data sources, query languages, functions, operators. Polars is a DataFrame library first; DataFusion is a planner and executor that also exposes a DataFrame API and full SQL. Versus Dask, which scales pandas across a cluster, DataFusion is single-node alone - clustering is Ballista, Spark acceleration is Comet.

Honest Limits

  • It is a library, not a service: no query endpoint; you embed the engine and build the serving layer, or adopt Ballista for distribution. Freedom, with an invoice attached.
  • datafusion-cli is explicitly a small utility, not a production shell, and has no official Docker image - the docs say to build one from source.
  • Format coverage is broad but not absolute: CSV, Parquet, JSON ship by default; Avro sits behind an optional feature flag in Cargo.toml.
  • The repo README prints no curated benchmark tables; benchmark questions point at external results, so measure on your own data.
  • APIs move: deprecation guidelines exist, and the docs pin datafusion = "55.1.0", so expect version bumps rather than forever-copyable snippets.

None of these limits are hidden: the architecture docs, rule reference, and test suite are unusually candid about the seams - exactly what you want from the layer your features flow through before they reach a model.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Apache DataFusion: SQL and DataFrame APIs, rule-based optimization, streaming Arrow execution, Parquet pushdown, and disk-backed spills - with two architecture diagrams built from the main branch.

entry.title: Apache Flink Under the Hood: A Source Tour of True Streaming, Event Time, and Exactly-Once State

link.title: Apache Flink Under the Hood: A Source Tour of True Streaming, Event Time, and Exactly-Once State

entry.content:
Most machine-learning systems treat streaming data as plumbing: events arrive in Kafka, a nightly batch job in Spark rebuilds aggregates, and the model serving tier reads whatever is freshest in Redis. Apache Flink attacks that gap differently. It is a streaming-first compute engine — its own README describes “a runtime that supports very high throughput and low event latency at the same time,” event-time and out-of-order processing “based on the Dataflow Model,” and “fault-tolerance with exactly-once processing guarantees.” Those are not marketing lines; each one maps to a specific subsystem you can read in the source.

That matters for AI infrastructure more than it first appears. Real-time feature computation is a stateful aggregation problem: per-user click counts over the last five minutes, rolling averages per device, session summaries keyed by entity — computed continuously, not rebuilt nightly, so the model at serving time sees features that are seconds old rather than hours old. Anomaly detection on telemetry is the same shape: windowed statistics compared against thresholds, where late and out-of-order events must still land in the right bucket. Continuous-learning data flows benefit too, because a consistent, replayable event flow with exactly-once state means a failed aggregation does not silently double-count training inputs. Flink’s windows, watermarks, and keyed state exist precisely for these jobs.

This post is a source tour, not a tutorial: we read the current master branch of apache/flink and map the path a record takes from your API calls to a running subtask, and the path a checkpoint takes from the coordinator to durable storage. Two diagrams anchor the walk — a system overview first, then a deeper internals map. One note before we start: Flink’s master has recently been reorganized, and the classic streaming API now lives inside flink-runtime rather than the older flink-streaming-java module. Every path and line number below was verified against the actual tree.

Overview: user code compiles to a StreamGraph, then a JobGraph; the JobManager schedules it onto TaskManager slots, where operator chains run and checkpoint barriers synchronize with the state backends.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • You start at the environment. StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment, L2178 hands back the local or cluster environment, and sources are attached with fromSource or socketTextStream.
  • Transformations are just calls on DataStream. DataStream, L111 exposes map, L422, flatMap, and keyBy, L274 — nothing runs yet; each call records a node in the logical operator graph.
  • The plan becomes executable in two hops. StreamGraph.getJobGraph, L1181 turns the logical graph into a JobGraph, L70 of deployable tasks.
  • The JobMaster owns your job. JobMaster, L155 is the RPC endpoint that builds the ExecutionGraph, L81 — now an interface — and drives it to completion.
  • Workers are TaskExecutors. TaskExecutor, L206 is the TaskManager-side RPC endpoint that offers slots and spawns subtasks on request.
  • Subtasks run fused operators. Each deployed task is a StreamTask, L216 executing an OperatorChain, L111, so records cross chained operators as method calls, not network hops.
  • Fault tolerance is a separate subsystem. The CheckpointCoordinator, L103 calls triggerCheckpoint, L575 periodically and CheckpointBarrier, L45 events flow with the data to align every operator.
  • State lands in a backend. For large keyed state, EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend, L98 keeps working set on disk; heap-sized state uses the HashMap backend.

Internals: job submission through the Dispatcher and REST endpoint, slot negotiation, ExecutionGraph scheduling, the network shuffle between ResultPartition and SingleInputGate, and the checkpoint and state layers.

The Life of a Job, From Submission to Slots

Submission is client-side code becoming cluster state. The Dispatcher, L170 accepts the JobGraph and spawns one JobMaster per job, while the WebMonitorEndpoint, L229 serves the REST API and dashboard you see in a Flink session cluster. The JobMaster then negotiates resources through DefaultDeclarativeSlotPool, L88, which tracks the slots each TaskExecutor has offered and matches them to the job’s declared demands.

Scheduling is where the logical graph becomes parallel. DefaultScheduler, L85 walks the ExecutionGraph’s ExecutionVertex, L60 instances — one per parallel subtask — and deploys them into assigned slots. On the worker side, TaskManagerRunner, L110 bootstraps the process. Data movement between subtasks is explicit: a task writes into a ResultPartition, L78, and the downstream SingleInputGate, L128 pulls buffers from it. Because a slow consumer stops pulling, back-pressure propagates upstream as full buffers rather than as dropped or queued records — the README’s “natural back-pressure” claim is literally this design.

Chaining deserves a second look because it is the main throughput lever in that design. The graph compiler fuses consecutive operators into a single task whenever parallelism and partitioning allow, and the OperatorChain wraps the fused operators so each record crosses an internal boundary as a plain method call. That removes serialization, thread hand-offs, and network round trips from the hot path — which is why a word-count job with a source, a flatMap, and an aggregate often runs as one chained task, while a keyBy boundary that genuinely requires a network shuffle is exactly where the chain gets cut and a ResultPartition appears.

Checkpointing: How Exactly-Once Survives Failure

The exactly-once guarantee is not magic; it is a two-party protocol between the job master and every subtask. The CheckpointCoordinator initiates a snapshot and special barrier events are injected into each input stream. When a StreamTask, L216 receives barriers on all inputs, it snapshots its operator state and acknowledges — the asynchronous path lives at triggerCheckpointAsync, L1538. The kind of snapshot travels with the trigger: CheckpointOptions, L40 tells each task whether it is taking a regular periodic snapshot or a different flavor, which is how one coordinator serves both routine persistence and savepoint-style requests. Because a barrier is just a RuntimeEvent, L45 traveling with the records, alignment semantics stay consistent even under back-pressure: the checkpoint divides the event flow into “before” and “after,” so state never mixes pre- and post-failure data. If a task fails, the coordinator discards the incomplete snapshot and the job restarts from the last completed one.

For feature-computation workloads this is the property that matters: an aggregation restart does not double-count the events that arrived during the failure. The barrier alignment is also what makes unaligned and incremental checkpointing possible without breaking the guarantee, though the master branch code behind those modes continues to evolve — treat anything beyond the basic aligned path as subject to change.

Event Time, Watermarks, and the State Layer

Event-time correctness rests on Watermark, L46 — a Serializable marker asserting that no earlier events should follow — and on window assigners like TumblingProcessingTimeWindows, L46 that bucket elements into fixed spans. When you need more control than map or flatMap, ProcessFunction, L52 gives you timers and direct state access. Watermarks ride the same buffers as records: sources emit them, each downstream task observes them to fire timers and close windows, and that is what keeps a five-minute feature window correct even when the input source delivers events late or out of order.

That state is typed and scoped. ValueState, L40 is the user-facing handle for one value per key, held inside a KeyedStateBackend, L36. Which backend you pick decides your memory story: the StateBackend, L81 interface has a heap implementation in HashMapStateBackend, L63 — fast, but snapshots serialize everything — and the RocksDB implementation, which spills to disk and supports incremental snapshots. A feature store aggregating millions of keys almost always wants RocksDB; a small session join may be happier on the heap backend.

From Install to Your First Model

The README is refreshingly concrete about requirements. Building from source needs a Unix-like environment (Linux, macOS, Cygwin, or WSL), Git, unzip, Maven 3.9.16, and Java 11, 17, or 21. Then:

git clone https://github.com/apache/flink.git
cd flink
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests -Djdk17 -Pjava17-target

That Java 17 profile is the default; the README documents -Djdk11 -Pjava11-target and -Djdk21 -Pjava21-target for the other JDKs, warns to set JAVA_HOME correctly, and estimates roughly ten minutes for the build, landing in build-target. From there, the README’s streaming example is your first running job: StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment(), env.socketTextStream(host, port), a flatMap that splits lines, keyBy, a TumblingProcessingTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) window, sum("count"), and env.execute(). It is a word count, but its skeleton is exactly a real-time feature job — swap the tokenizer for per-entity aggregations and the socket source for a connector, and you are computing serving features.

One practical note: most connectors are no longer in this repository. The README lists them as externalized Apache repos — flink-connector-kafka, flink-connector-jdbc, flink-connector-elasticsearch, and a dozen more — so a production dataflow graph usually involves adding those dependencies to your project rather than building them here. The SQL layer lives in the flink-table module tree if you prefer declarative streaming queries over the DataStream API, and per-key incremental views are also the specialty of engines like RisingWave, which make a different trade-off between latency and expressiveness.

Honest Limits

  • Build friction is real. A Unix-like environment is required for building, the pinned Maven 3.9.16 is strict, and the README’s own estimate is about ten minutes before you have written a line of code.
  • The API surface is mid-migration. On master, the classic streaming classes now sit in flink-runtime, the old flink-streaming-java module is largely a husk, and a new DataStream V2 API (flink-datastream-api, with NonKeyedPartitionStream and KeyedPartitionStream) is growing alongside. Code you write today targets a moving tree.
  • Connectors are separate projects. Kafka, JDBC, Elasticsearch, and friends live in their own repositories with their own release cycles — one more version-matrix to manage.
  • Operational weight. Exactly-once state buys you a distributed-systems surface: checkpoint storage to configure, savepoint compatibility to preserve across upgrades, and a cluster (or a Kubernetes operator) to run — far heavier than a single-process analytics engine that fits on one node.
  • No free lunch on latency claims. The README promises throughput and low event latency, but the right numbers depend entirely on your window sizes, state sizes, and backend choice; we deliberately cite no benchmarks here because none appear in the repository.

For an AI stack, the honest summary is this: Flink is the right tool when features or alerts must be stateful, event-time-correct, and continuously consistent with model serving — and it is heavier than you need when a simple consumer writing aggregates into Redis, or a batch reconstruction in Spark, would do. Read the source with the second diagram open; the barrier protocol and the slot economy explain most of what production Flink feels like.
